title: Professional feature on flexible-work trial evidence

job.buyer: Editor of a South African management publication
job.request: Turn the supplied research summary, employer survey and expert interview into a 1,000-1,400 word evidence-backed feature for managers.

source_documents.citation: Maseko, L. & Pillay, R. (2026). Hybrid work and knowledge-team outcomes: a 12-month field study.
source_documents.text:
RESEARCH SUMMARY
Sample: 18 knowledge-work teams across three South African firms.
Key finding: teams using two structured remote days per week showed no statistically significant decline in measured output over 12 months.
Key finding: voluntary turnover was lower in the hybrid group, but the study was observational and cannot establish that hybrid work caused the retention difference.
Limitation: participating firms were professional-services businesses; results should not be generalised to all sectors.

source_documents.citation: Workplace Futures SA. (2026). Employer pulse survey, Q2.
source_documents.text:
EMPLOYER SURVEY
61% of 214 responding employers reported that managers remain concerned about coordination and mentoring in hybrid teams.
47% reported that they had changed meeting norms or documentation practices after introducing hybrid work.
The survey is self-reported and is not a productivity experiment.

source_documents.citation: Interview with Dr Amina Patel, organisational psychologist, 3 August 2026.
source_documents.text:
EXPERT INTERVIEW
Dr Amina Patel: "The useful question is not whether hybrid work is universally better. It is which tasks, teams and management practices make flexibility workable."
Patel cautioned that firms should track output, onboarding and collaboration rather than relying only on employee preference surveys.

constraints: Do not claim hybrid work causes higher productivity or retention.
Distinguish survey perceptions from experimental evidence.
Publication remains subject to human editorial review.
